titleStmt.title: Chapter 7 — The Late Antique Transition — Kullaba - E-Anna instances III

div.p: Late antiquity is a major pivot in human history. Then, the anti-E-Anna tradition, which was attested earlier in works like the Epic of Gilgamesh and the early Jewish tradition, emerges as a major culture-shaping force with the rise of Christianity and then Islam. The sections of this chapter are not a continuous history but a series of snapshots where the Abrahamic anti-E-Anna stance appears at its most clear and consequential. Section 7.1, treats the textual epicenter of this stance, in the Book of Revelation. The subsequent two sections show how the only tangible immediate effect of Abrahamic Faiths hegemony is to drive the E-Anna into the black, without substantial changes (the deeper impacts take much longer to make themselves felt). In a detour to India, the next two sections depict the road not taken by the now monotheistic Europe and Middle-East. Finally, in the last section of this chapter, we discuss a quasi-red resurgence of the E-Anna in Byzantium under Justinian. This last section is a foreshadowing of the Sargonitis episodes discussed in the next chapter. As in the previous two chapters, the numbers in square brackets in section headings refer back to the table in Chapter 4.

div.head: 7.1 [12] The Book of Revelation — Unveiling the Whore and the E-Anna-Free Utopia
7.1.1 Assyriology, the Religionsgeschichtliche Schule, and Marxist Paradigms
div.p: The apocalyptic imagery of the Whore of Babylon in the Book of Revelation does not emerge from a theological vacuum; it is the culminating expression of a deep, prophetic resistance to the Ishtarian sovereignty engine. Its immediate literary antecedent is the prophet Nahum’s searing denunciation of Nineveh, the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, which he explicitly castigates as a harlot and mistress of sorceries operating a state-sponsored matrix of mimetic terror (see Section 6.1 in the previous chapter). For centuries, however, the precise mythological dimensions of this biblical archetype remained obscured.

This changed dramatically from the mid-19th century onward, as the rapid progress of Assyriology resurrected the primary texts of the ancient Near East. Recognizing these striking parallels, the German Religionsgeschichtliche Schule (History of Religions school)—led by figures like Hermann Gunkel—systematically mapped the Book of Revelation against Mesopotamian mythological material, demonstrating how archaic combat myths and the terrifying, dualistic nature of the Near Eastern martial-erotic goddess heavily informed John of Patmos's apocalyptic vocabulary.Hermann Gunkel, Schöpfung und Chaos in Urzeit und Endzeit: Eine religionsgeschichtliche Untersuchung über Gen 1 und Ap Joh 12 (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1895), pp. 379-398. Gunkel pioneered the comparative method that permanently linked the apocalyptic beasts and the Babylonian imagery of Revelation to archaic Mesopotamian chaos-combat myths (Chaoskampf) and the overarching Near Eastern imperial ideologies. Following World War II, as scholarship took a decidedly materialist turn, the text was radically re-read through a Marxist-inspired paradigm. Spearheaded by scholars such as Richard A. Horsley, this school interpreted Revelation's denunciation of Babylon primarily as a masterful propaganda attack against Roman imperialism. In this view, the Whore was simply an allegorical cipher for Rome's exploitative political economy and the rapacious extraction of wealth from its provincial peripheries.Richard A. Horsley, Jesus and Empire: The Kingdom of God and the New World Disorder (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2003), p. 134. Horsley states: Revelation 17–18 is a masterful propaganda attack against Rome imperialism, unmasking the 'glorious' empire as a predatory whore who seduces the local elites into collaboration and slaughters those who resist. As we shall see in Chapter 9, this Marxian approach was subsequently challenged by intersectional gender-studies critiques in recent decades.

div.head: 7.1.2 The Prophetic Lineage and the Second Temple Predecessors
div.p: The prophetic language of Revelation does not stand isolated; as pointed out above, it takes its rightful place in a continuous, millennia-long lineage of Kullaba-side resistance against the E-Anna's mythology. It belongs to the same structural tradition as Gilgamesh violently repudiating Ishtar's hieros gamos, Zarathustra demoting the martial Indo-Iranian deities to demonic daivas, and the Parashurama Brahmins mythologically annihilating the volatile Kshatriya warlords (see subsection 6.4.5 below).

In parallel to the mainstream Second Temple Jewish anti-E-Anna stream of the Old Testament, the anti-Ishtarian language of monotheism was also being enriched in non-canonical traditions like the Enochic literature. In particular, one leader of the fallen angels in 1 Enoch, Azazel, is described as bringing down to earth the exact attributes of Ishtar: lethal weapons and erotic ornaments. The text explicitly links martial violence with sexual seduction:

cit.quote: And Azazel taught men to make swords, and knives, and shields, and breastplates, and made known to them the metals of the earth and the art of working them, and bracelets, and ornaments, and the use of antimony, and the beautifying of the eyelids, and all kinds of costly stones, and all colouring tinctures.
cit.bibl: R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), p. 14.

div.p: Furthermore, the giants (Nephilim) fathered by the fallen Watchers upon human women are transparent mythological references to the BDMB archetype, violent martial warlords explicitly prefiguring the biblical Nimrod. By connecting the origin of weapons, cosmetics, and the resulting charismatic warlords entirely to a rebellion of fallen angels, this tradition thoroughly demonized the E-Anna engine, cementing its complete repudiation in the apocalyptic imagination.

div.head: 7.1.3 The Whore and the E-Anna-Free Utopia
div.p: The subsequent (first century AD) Book of Revelation pushes this Kullaba logic to its absolute eschatological extreme. Beyond merely critiquing Rome (or apostate Jerusalem as Fundamentalist Calvinist exegesis would have itFor the preterist interpretation common in certain Reformed and Fundamentalist Calvinist exegesis, which identifies the Whore of Babylon as apostate first-century Jerusalem rather than Rome, see David Chilton, The Days of Vengeance: An Exposition of the Book of Revelation (Fort Worth: Dominion Press, 1987), pp. 421-426.), the text envisions a reality where the dual sovereignty synthesis is no longer necessary. The Book of Revelation achieves a critical ideological milestone by unambiguously tying the Whore to both martial kingship and ritualized fornication (porneia)—the defining attributes of the Ishtarian paradigm. The apocalyptic text strips away the grandeur of the imperial state to expose the raw, intoxicating mimetic mechanism beneath. This nexus of royal power and erotic seduction is explicitly detailed in the seventeenth chapter:

cit.quote: Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication, and the inhabitants of the earth were made drunk with the wine of her fornication. [...] And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast which was full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, having in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the filthiness of her fornication. And on her forehead a name was written: MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.

div.p: In the New Jerusalem (Rev 21), there is explicitly no temple—and therefore no E-Anna precinct to generate martial-erotic power. It is a society governed entirely by the direct, unmediated presence of the Paternal Lawgiver (the Father) and the innocent son (the Lamb). This vision constitutes an explicit, uncompromising declaration of war on the E-Anna paradigm. In the minds of the original apocalyptic writers, this definitive metaphysical conflict was undoubtedly anticipated as a near-term eschatological event—a sudden, cosmic intervention that would literally obliterate the imperial martial-erotic machine. Instead, as the parousia was delayed, this radical anti-E-Anna manifesto became increasingly obscure and yet remain securely encoded within the canonical scripture of the early Christian movement. As the church transitioned from a persecuted sect into the institutional bedrock of the empire, the immediate, revolutionary potency of this vision decayed. By the Early Middle Ages, its original structural diagnosis was no longer fully understood; its primary concrete effect was simply to drive the E-Anna engine underground, forcing it to operate covertly in the black (see Middle Eastern parallel in the next two sections). While there were still sporadic, localized prophetic attacks against martial-erotic royal transgression—such as the fiery Irish monk Saint Columbanus assailing the lupanarium (brothel) of the Merovingian courtIan Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms 450-751 (London: Longman, 1994), p. 133., or John Chrysostom denouncing the Empress Eudoxia as a new JezebelJ. N. D. Kelly, Golden Mouth: The Story of John Chrysostom—Ascetic, Preacher, Bishop (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1995), p. 225.—the all-encompassing, anti-kingship structural critique embodied by the Whore of Babylon was largely in the process of being lost to mainstream political theology.

div.head: 7.1.4 The Sleepwalking Resurrection of the Utopia
div.p: Yet this apocalyptic blueprint for an E-Anna-free society proved resilient enough to survive its 1,000-year eclipse, throughout the Middle Ages. In the 16th century, it provided the precise structural code for the radical Protestant republics of the early modern era. It was this specific vision that drove the architectural and legal engineering of John Calvin's Geneva, the mercantile republic of Amsterdam, and the Puritan commonwealth of 17th-century Boston. By violently purging the altars, banning theatrical excess, and attempting to eradicate the BDMB archetype, these Protestant experiments laid the foundational cultural groundwork for the liberal modern state—a system that attempts (with varying degrees of success) to govern purely through constitutional law, rational commerce, and individual rights, representing the ultimate, secularized triumph of the Kullaba.

The strange paradox of early modern Protestantism is that it conducted a massive, systemic anti-E-Anna crusade across Europe in a state of ideological sleepwalking. It successfully dismantled the semi-covert Ishtarian machinery of the feudal nobility and the sacramental majesty of the Catholic Church, yet it never explicitly resurrected the full, anti-kingship, anti-martial-erotic meaning of the Whore of Babylon archetype. This conceptual blind spot was primarily due to the Reformers' polemical equation of the Whore exclusively with the Papacy. By locking the apocalyptic harlot into a narrow anti-clerical cipher, Protestant theologians structurally blinded themselves to the deeper, thermodynamic reality of the E-Anna engine. They waged a Kullaba-driven war on idolatry without fully comprehending the martial-erotic physics of the very idolatry they sought to destroy.

This sleepwalking dynamic is vividly illustrated in the tragedy of the Salem witch trials. In 1692, the agrarian, deeply puritanical residents of Salem Village (Salem-West) lashed out at the increasingly mercantile, cosmopolitan, and wealthy elite of Salem Town (Salem-East). At its core, the hysteria was a desperate, unarticulated reaction by a pure Kullaba community against what they dimly perceived as an emergent, neo-E-Anna commercial aristocracy operating in the black.Paul Boyer and Stephen Nissenbaum, Salem Possessed: The Social Origins of Witchcraft (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1974), pp. 86-103. Boyer and Nissenbaum conclusively map the socio-economic geography of the accusations, demonstrating that the agrarian traditionalists of Salem Village systematically accused the ascending, mercantile elites associated with Salem Town. However, because the Calvinist theologians of Boston—such as Cotton Mather—lacked the structural vocabulary to identify this as a predictable mimetic crisis driven by the Ishtarian allure of wealth, exclusivity and ornaments (such as those enumerated in the above mentioned 1 Enoch), they could only process the conflict through a literalist lens of diabolical pacts and spectral evidence. Unable to decipher the fundamental anti-E-Anna urges of the accusers, the Boston elite eventually had to forcibly shut down the movement to maintain order. In doing so, they squandered a profound opportunity: instead of leveraging the crisis to reinforce a sophisticated theological rejection of this new, covert idolatry, they effectively crushed the last organic spasm of the Protestant Kullaba utopia, paving the way for the secular liberal state to ultimately succumb to the very mimetic forces it failed to name. Had this opportunity not been missed, Girard would have been anticipated by nearly three centuries and the subsequent history of Western Culture would have been radically altered.

div.head: 7.2 [13] Sassanid Persia — Zoroastrianism and the Last Red Synthesis
7.2.1 The Return of the Repressed: From the Gathas to the Younger Avesta
div.p: In our examination of early Indo-Iranian dynamics (Section 5.4), we observed that the prophet Zarathustra engineered a radical, puritanical theological revolution. In the Gathas, the oldest layers of the Avesta, Zarathustra violently purged the overt martial-erotic deities of the Indo-Iranian warband, demoting them to malignant daivasFor the demonization of ancient martial deities, see Mary Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism, Volume I: The Early Period (Leiden: Brill, 1975), p. 85. Boyce observes that Indra, the paramount warrior god of the Vedic pantheon, was explicitly demoted to the arch-demon Indar in the Zoroastrian Vendidad, reflecting a total theological repudiation of the martial Männerbund. and elevating the supreme, paternal singularity of Ahura Mazda. However, as the Hammurabi synthesis conclusively demonstrated (Section 5.3), a purely Kullaba-centric theology could not be expected to sustainably govern a massive territorial empire on its own (at least in the first and second millennia BCE); it inevitably lacked the contagious charismatic gravitational pull required to bind a martial apparatus and extract compliance. Consequently, the repressed E-Anna engine inevitably returned. In the so-called Younger Avesta, the martial-erotic dynamic unmistakably reasserts itself, most notably through the figure of Anahita (Aredvi Sura Anahita), the Strong, Immaculate Waters. Despite Zarathustra's original vision, the ancient Near Eastern engine of the martial-erotic goddess proved sociopolitically indispensable.For the diachronic evolution of the Avestan texts and the gradual reintegration of pre-Zoroastrian deities into the Younger Avesta, see Prods Oktor Skjærvø, The Avesta as Source for the Early History of the Iranians, in The Indo-Aryans of Ancient South Asia, ed. George Erdosy (Berlin: De Gruyter, 1995), pp. 155-176. and Almut Hintze, The Avesta in the Parthian Period, in Das Partherreich und seine Zeugnisse, ed. Josef Wiesehöfer (Stuttgart: Franz Steiner, 1998), pp. 147-161.

div.head: 7.2.2 The First Integrated Monotheizing Synthesis
div.p: This reintegration makes Zoroastrianism an extraordinarily pivotal case study: it is the first fully integrated, monotheizing religion—complete with formal dogma, standardized rituals, sacred scriptures, and a rigorous, hierarchical priesthood—to explicitly adopt the dual sovereignty synthesis. While the Achaemenid Empire and the subsequent Parthian Empire undoubtedly utilized this paradigm, the scarcity of their internal textual and theological records limits our granular reconstruction. It is in the Sassanid Empire (224–651 CE) that this structural synthesis is spectacularly and unambiguously attested. The Sassanid state engineered an orthodox, institutionalized balance between the strict purity laws of the cosmos and the visceral, kinetic power of the battlefield.For comprehensive historical overviews of the Sassanid Empire and its institutional synthesis of Zoroastrian orthodoxy with imperial administration, see Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia: The Rise and Fall of an Empire (London: I.B. Tauris, 2009); and Josef Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia, trans. Azizeh Azodi (London: I.B. Tauris, 2001), pp. 153-221.

div.head: 7.2.3 The Sassanid Culmination: Ahura Mazda and Anahita
div.p: In the Sassanid formulation, the Kullaba was managed by the Magi (the Zoroastrian clergy), who administered the rigid purity laws, the fire temples, and the universalizing theology of asha (cosmic truth and order) under the supreme father-god Ahura Mazda. This provided the glove of predictable, righteous administration. Conversely, the kinetic fist of the state—the BDMB energy of the Šāhānšāh (King of Kings)—was sustained by the E-Anna mechanism. In monumental rock reliefs, such as those at Naqsh-e Rustam and Taq-e Bostan, the king is repeatedly depicted receiving the khvarenah (the divine royal glory or martial mandateFor an analysis of the visual representation of the khvarenah in Sassanid investiture reliefs, see Matthew P. Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth: Art and Ritual of Kingship Between Rome and Sasanian Iran (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2009), pp. 57-61.) not only from Ahura Mazda but prominently from Anahita.

The goddess, heavily syncretized over centuries with the Mesopotamian Ishtar, effectively operates as the divine consort and martial sponsor of the warlord. She validates his right to exercise lethal force and conquer. The Sassanid state explicitly required both: the Magi to declare the king's rule lawful and cosmically ordered, and Anahita to grant him the terrifying, mimetic invincibility required to crush Rome and the steppe nomads.For the geopolitical necessity of martial prestige during the protracted conflicts with Rome and nomadic frontier confederations, see James Howard-Johnston, East Rome, Sasanian Persia and the End of Antiquity (Aldershot: Ashgate, 2006).

The cosmic dualism of Zoroastrianism (Good vs. Evil) is often considered one of its defining features, but it should not be confused with the Kullaba-E-Anna dichotomy outlined here. Within Sassanian royal ideology, Zoroastrian dualism is entirely within the realm of theological justification. It is simply a starker formulation of the notion of righteousness that was already present in the Hammurabi synthesis. Both Ahura Mazda (Kullaba) and Anahita (E-Anna) are on the side of Good fighting against the cosmic evil of Ahriman. The Magi fight Ahriman through ritual purity, law, and truth (asha), while the Šāhānšāh and Anahita fight Ahriman through the kinetic, mimetic violence of the cavalry charge. The Sassanid state harnessed both functions under the banner of the Good Religion. However, Ahriman also remained an implicit threat that the Magi could wield against a rogue Shah by rejecting him on the side of the druj, thus creating a devastating coalition of the meek against him. For the Magi, this is the nuclear option, but it is always useful as an implicit threat. This tool appears to have been used already in the Achaemenid period during the reign of Darius the Great, as the Behistun Inscription (no doubt largely written by the Magi faction which supported Darius) attests. By calling the deposed ruler Smerdis/Bardiya a man of the lie the writers of the inscription firmly reject him into the realm of absolute condemnation.In the Behistun Inscription, Darius the Great systematically employs the theological concept of the Lie (druj / Old Persian drauga) to delegitimize his rivals, declaring: The Lie made them rebellious, so that these men deceived the people. See Roland G. Kent, Old Persian: Grammar, Texts, Lexicon (New Haven: American Oriental Society, 1953), DB IV.34, p. 131. Darius portrays the usurper Smerdis (Bardiya) fundamentally as a practitioner of the Lie. Did some among the Magi, like the famous Kartir,Kartir (or Kerdīr) was an exceptionally powerful high priest (mobed) of the early Sassanid Empire who served under multiple successive Shahs in the third century CE. He consolidated Zoroastrian orthodoxy, centralized the religious administration, and systematically persecuted rival faiths like Manichaeism, Christianity, and Buddhism, wielding unprecedented political influence for a non-royal figure. See Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia: The Rise and Fall of an Empire (London: I.B. Tauris, 2009), pp. 74-77. once entertain the idea of a Zoroastrian Republic of Iran entirely free of the need for a potentially troublesome Shah? We may imagine it, based on the tone of certain inscriptions,In his monumental rock inscription at the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht, Kartir breaks with precedent by leaving propaganda of his own—a privilege normally reserved strictly for the King of Kings. His boastful tone, detailing his consolidation of the priesthood, execution of state policy, and establishment of sacred fires, projects an authority that directly rivals royal prerogatives, hinting at the theoretical possibility of a purely magian administration. See Prods Oktor Skjærvø, Kerdīr, in Encyclopædia Iranica, Vol. XV, Fasc. 6 (2011), pp. 608-628. but no source attests that any such idea was ever seriously considered.

div.head: 7.2.4 The Last Bastion of the Red
div.p: Crucially, Sassanid Persia represents the absolute terminus of the red E-Anna in the ancient Near Eastern and Western world. It was the final major imperial power to operate a state religion that officially and overtly worshipped a female deity of martial-erotic power alongside the paternal god of order. While Rome had transitioned its Ishtarian engine into the black under Augustus (and even more so under Constantine), the Sassanid state openly celebrated the Ishtarian dynamic of sovereignty justification right up until its catastrophic geopolitical collapse in the 7th century CE. Its conquerors, the armies of Islam, brought with them the ultimate, uncompromising formulation of the Abrahamic Faiths. As will be explored in Section 7.3, Islam forced the E-Anna engine permanently into the covert sphere, irrevocably altering the architectural visibility of the dual sovereignty engine across Eurasia.

div.head: 7.3 [14] Islamic Kingship — The Caliphate and the Walled-Off E-Anna
7.3.1 The Caliphal Model as the Sassanian Inheritance
div.p: The geopolitical collapse of the Sassanid Empire under the weight of the Arab conquests did not eradicate the underlying thermodynamics of Eurasian statecraft; rather, the emerging Caliphal model of the Umayyad and Abbasid empiresFor foundational analyses of the structural evolution of the early Islamic state and its transition from a nomadic conquest movement to a sedentary, bureaucratic empire, see Fred M. Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1981), and Hugh Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates: The Islamic Near East from the Sixth to the Eleventh Century (London: Longman, 1986). essentially absorbed and transferred the Sassanian model of kingship into the world of the black (the covert, unacknowledged sphere). Because Islam is a strict Abrahamic faith, the official, state-sponsored worship of a martial-erotic female deity—the red (overt) manifestation of the E-Anna, such as Anahita or Ishtar—was strictly forbidden and ideologically impossible. The public, religious face of the state (the Kullaba) was entirely monopolized by the abstract, paternal majesty of Allah, administered by the ulama through the strict legalism of the shari'a. However, to operate a massive, multi-ethnic territorial empire stretching from Spain to India, the Caliphs structurally required the immense, charismatic gravitational pull of the BDMB archetype.

div.head: 7.3.2 The Minimalistic Solution and the Physical Barrier
div.p: Faced with the necessity of maintaining the E-Anna's martial-erotic engine without officially acknowledging it, the Islamic solution proved to be much cruder and more minimalistic than the Christian approach. As discussed in relation to René Girard's insights (see Chapter 3), the Christian ideal attempts, however imperfectly, a profound internal dismantling of mimetic violence resulting (hopefully) in personal regeneration. Islam, in this specific structural regard, takes its cue much more from the Pharisaic Judaism of the Talmud. Instead of seeking a radical, metaphysical deconstruction of human desire, it relies on erecting physical and legal barriers. The Islamic version of the Kullaba utilizes institutions such as the hijab and the high, impenetrable walls of the royal household to simply hide rather than dismantle the psychological footprint of the E-Anna. The charismatic, erotic energy necessary to elevate the sovereign is pushed out of the public square and sequestered entirely within the private palace.For the historical emergence and political function of the Islamic harem—particularly its institutionalization during the Abbasid caliphate and its zenith under the Ottoman Empire as a secluded, highly structured locus of dynastic reproduction and sequestered charismatic power—see Leslie P. Peirce, The Imperial Harem: Women and Sovereignty in the Ottoman Empire (New York: Oxford University Press, 1993), pp. 3-17; and Nadia Maria El Cheikh, Revisiting the Abbasid Harems, Journal of Middle East Women's Studies 1, no. 3 (2005): 1-19. Nonetheless, it remains present in everyone's mind.

div.head: 7.3.3 The Etymology of Harem
div.p: This structural sequestration is perfectly encapsulated in the linguistic reality of the harem. It is noteworthy that the word harem shares its etymological root with ḥaram, the Arabic term for what is strictly forbidden or illicit. However, the linguistic root traces back to an older, more archaic spatial concept meaning separate or cut-off—a concept virtually identical to the Latin sacer (that which is set apart from the profane, hence sacred). Far from being ḥaram in the sense of a sinful abomination, the harem is in fact walled off, which is to say, it is sacred, like the Byzantine sacrum cubiculumIn the Byzantine court, the sacrum cubiculum (sacred bedchamber) functioned as the restricted, inviolable core of the emperor's private residence. While it was explicitly designated as sacred (sacrum) to denote its absolute segregation from the profane public sphere and to generate sovereign awe, it did not constitute a harem in the Islamic sense of a sequestered, polygamous space exclusively for women. Instead, it was an exclusive center of political charisma and intimate access, heavily guarded and administered by eunuch officials (cubicularii). For an analysis of the spatial and ideological sacredness of the Byzantine imperial chambers, see Shaun Tougher, The Eunuch in Byzantine History and Society (London: Routledge, 2008), pp. 44-46.. It functions as the physically sequestered precinct of the E-Anna, covert yet known to all, generating the necessary mimetic awe and exclusivity that fuels the sovereign's power, completely out of sight of the puritanical (but complicit) ulama.

div.head: 7.3.4 The Tiniest of Fig-Leaves
div.p: Consequently, it is no surprise to observe that this tiniest of architectural fig-leaves changes nothing thermodynamically. The Caliph, and virtually every successful Muslim warlord, Sultan, or Emir after him, remains a pure, unadulterated product of the Mesopotamian BDMB tradition. The transition from the Sassanid Šāhānšāh to the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad is the ultimate historical manifestation of a famous literary axiom. As a character in Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa's seminal novel Il Gattopardo declares regarding political revolutions:

cit.quote: Everything has to change so that everything will be like before.
cit.bibl: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa, The Leopard, trans. Archibald Colquhoun (New York: Pantheon Books, 1960), p. 40.

div.p: The outward iconography was fundamentally altered to conform to strict Abrahamic monotheism, but the dual sovereignty engine of the Middle East continued to hum with frictionless efficiency, driving the great Islamic empires of the medieval and early modern world.

div.head: 7.4 [15-16] Hindu Kingship — The Exoteric Synthesis and the Esoteric Tension
7.4.1 The Post-Mauryan Restoration and the Gupta Synthesis
div.p: The classical Hindu theology of kingship emerged from a profound structural crisis. The Mauryan Empire, particularly under Ashoka, had attempted an unprecedented experiment in statecraft: ruling a vast subcontinental empire through an almost exclusively First Function, non-violent universalism (Buddhist dharma) and a structural bureaucracy imitated from the Achaemenid Empire.Romila Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1961), pp. 126-128. Thapar explicitly traces the administrative centralization, the use of imperial edicts on monumental stone pillars, and the overall bureaucratic architecture of the Mauryan state to Achaemenid Persian precedents. Stripped of the martial-erotic E-Anna engine, this hyper-pacified model proved thermodynamically unsustainable over the longue durée, resulting in imperial fragmentation. In the ensuing centuries, as the subcontinent sought a new equilibrium, it built upon the archaic, Kuru-Panchala Brahmin orthopraxy, forging a robust, hybridized architecture of power that achieved its classical expression in the Mahabharata and triumphed permanently during the Gupta period.

This classical Hindu kingship is uniquely fascinating because it deliberately bifurcated the dual sovereignty engine into two parallel tracks: an exoteric (public) synthesis and an esoteric (covert) state of tension. The exoteric formulation is a textbook manifestation of the Hammurabi-style synthesis operating overtly in the red, structurally identical to the Sassanian model discussed in Section 7.2.

div.head: 7.4.2 The Red State in Action: Durga and the Wodeyars of Mysore
div.p: In the exoteric public sphere, the Kullaba apparatus was monopolized by orthodox Brahmin castes serving the paternal, order-preserving god Vishnu (or equivalent high-gods acting in a maintaining capacity). This priesthood provided the glove of predictable cosmic law and administrative rigor. However, to wield the kinetic violence necessary for territorial sovereignty, the orthodox Brahmins explicitly authorized the public worship of Durga, the fierce, demon-slaying manifestation of the goddess. The king derived his martial fitness and BDMB prestige directly from her blessing.

This ancient thermodynamic arrangement was so resilient that it survived virtually intact into the mid-20th century in the princely state of Mysore. Until 1947 (and ceremonially up to the present day), the Wodeyar monarchs orchestrated the grand Navaratri (Dasara) festival—a spectacular, state-sponsored theatrical display of royal and martial power blessed by the goddess Chamundeshwari (a local form of Durga). Crucially, the administration of the state and the strict orthopraxic officiating of these very rituals were managed by orthodox Vaishnavite Brahmin castes serving as viziers and administrators—specifically, the Madhvas and the Shri-Vaishnavas.For a comprehensive anthropological analysis of the royal Navaratri festival in Mysore and its function in regenerating the king's sovereignty through the goddess, overseen by strict Brahmanic orthopraxy, see C. J. Fuller, The Camphor Flame: Popular Hinduism and Society in India (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1992), pp. 108-127. The Kullaba administrators (the Vaishnava Brahmins) literally held the keys to the ritual deployment of the E-Anna energy (the goddess's martial blessing upon the king), achieving a perfectly balanced, overt red synthesis.

div.head: 7.4.3 The Esoteric Tension: Tantra and the Quest for siddhi
div.p: While the exoteric synthesis pacified the populace and legitimized public administration, the BDMB monarch frequently sought an additional raw, unmediated source of terrifying power—a mimetic surplus that bypassed the strict purity laws of the orthodox Brahmins. This necessity generated the esoteric, Tantric track of Hindu kingship. Operating in a semi-covert, black sphere (functionally analogous to the Greco-Roman mystery cults, but intimately tied to royal power), kings patronized left-hand Tantric rituals centered around transgressive avatars of Shakti.

These rituals were administered not by the orthodox Kullaba, but by non-Brahmin, antinomian ascetics (such as the Kapalikas or Nath yogis). Through the deliberate violation of orthodox purity taboos (involving meat, alcohol, and ritualized sexual union), these esoteric practices generated immense charismatic and magical capital known as siddhi.David Gordon White brilliantly documents how the transgressive, alchemical, and sexual practices of Tantric ascetics were heavily patronized by medieval Indian kings to generate siddhi, securing their martial invulnerability and terrifying political prestige. See David Gordon White, The Alchemical Body: Siddha Traditions in Medieval India (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1996), pp. 120-135. The king weaponized this esoteric siddhi to secure invulnerability in battle and project a terrifying, sorcerous aura over his rivals. Because this mechanism directly subverted the official order, the esoteric track existed in a state of perpetual, carefully managed tension with the orthodox Brahminical establishment.

div.head: 7.4.4 The Indo-European Bifurcation of the Goddess
div.p: The dual tracks of Hindu kingship reveal a profound feature of the Indo-European cultural matrix: the bifurcation of the holistic, ancient Near Eastern Ishtar archetype. When the E-Anna paradigm migrated into Indo-European environments—societies characterized by much stricter, patriarchal First Function priesthoods—the terrifying totality of the Mesopotamian goddess was frequently split to make her sociopolitically manageable.

In Greece, as noted in Section 6.3, Ishtar's martial violence was sanitized into the virginal, civic warrior Athena, while her erotic, mimetic frenzy was quarantined into Aphrodite. India executed the exact same structural bifurcation. The overt, exoteric synthesis utilized Durga (the virginal, demon-slaying warrior-maiden who fights but does not copulate) to grant legitimate territorial sovereignty. Conversely, the covert, esoteric tension utilized Shakti and the Mahavidyas (overtly sexual, transgressive, and horrific goddesses) to generate raw, antinomian siddhi. The Indian dual sovereignty engine thus operated on both cylinders simultaneously: maintaining the glove in the daylight, while fueling the fist in the shadows of the cremation ground.

div.head: 7.4.5 The Kullaba-only temptation: Parashurama
div.p: The Kullaba did not always restrict itself to passive containment. At certain historical junctures, orthodox Brahminical factions seemingly harbored the ambition to establish a pure Kullaba state—an overarching, Kshatriya-free utopian society stripped entirely of the E-Anna martial sovereign. This ideological temptation is probably preserved in the mythology of Parashurama, the warrior-Brahmin avatar of Vishnu.For an extensive analysis of the Parashurama myth as a mythological encoding of intense socio-political conflict between the Brahmin and Kshatriya classes, particularly highlighting the Bhargava clan's militant defense of priestly supremacy, see Robert P. Goldman, Gods, Priests, and Warriors: The Bhrgus of the Mahabharata (New York: Columbia University Press, 1977), pp. 130-145. According to the Mahabharata and the Puranas, Parashurama systematically annihilated the corrupt Kshatriya caste twenty-one times, cleansing the earth of their volatile, BDMB-like martial excess to restore an absolute, Brahminical dharma. This narrative structurally mirrors the ambitions we can perhaps attribute to figures like the Sassanian high priest Kartir (see Section 7.2), whom we have imagined harboring the theocratic fantasy of a Zoroastrian Republic of Iran. Parashurama would then be the memory of equivalent theocratic dreams in the Indian context.

It is noteworthy that Parashurama is traditionally credited with creating the Konkan coastThe mythological tradition of Parashurama forcing the ocean to recede by throwing his axe to reclaim the Konkan and Malabar coasts is widely interpreted as an etiology for the historical migration and establishment of orthodox Brahminical agrarian communities in the region. See D. D. Kosambi, Myth and Reality: Studies in the Formation of Indian Culture (Bombay: Popular Prakashan, 1962), pp. 110-115. by demanding the sea recede to reveal virgin land. This localized geographic myth likely encodes the historical memory of an attempt by orthodox Brahmin communities to establish an isolated, Kshatriya-free agrarian utopia in a remote periphery, safely distanced from the thermodynamic turbulence of the central Gangetic and Deccan warring states. Ultimately, however, a pure Brahminical state proved unsustainable against external kinetic threats. Consequently, the orthodox establishment co-opted Parashurama into the standard Dashavatara (the ten primary avatarsThe Dashavatara represents the classical Hindu theological framework standardizing the ten primary descents of Vishnu, serving as a powerful orthodox tool to assimilate disparate regional and martial cults under a unified Brahminical umbrella. See Gavin Flood, An Introduction to Hinduism (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996), pp. 116-118. of Vishnu). Positioned safely in the mythological past, the Brahmin-who-slaughters-kings functions as an enduring ideological deterrent—a latent nuclear threat brandished by the Kullaba against any potential rogue Kshatriya monarch, much like the Magi could wield the threat of excommunication into the realm of the druj to deter a rogue Shah.

div.head: 7.5 [17] Byzantium under Justinian — The Covert E-Anna and the Empress from the Hippodrome
7.5.1 The Historiographical Anomaly of the Circus Empresses
div.p: The reign of Justinian I (527–565 CE) represents the apogee of the Early Byzantine Empire. Justinian is universally celebrated as the ultimate architect of the Christian Kullaba. Through the monumental compilation of the Corpus Juris Civilis and the construction of the Hagia Sophia, he projected an awe-inspiring, Apollonian aura of absolute legal, bureaucratic, and theological order. Yet, embedded at the very apex of this hyper-orthodox, rigidly hierarchical state lay a profound sociological anomaly that has baffled historians for centuries.

Justinian, the most powerful man in the world, shattered centuries of Roman legal precedent to marry Theodora—a woman of the lowest possible social stratum, a former actress, dancer, and erotic performer from the Hippodrome. Compounding this anomaly, his supreme military commander, Belisarius, married Antonina, a woman with an almost identical, scandalous background in the theatrical demi-monde. Traditional historiography has struggled to articulate a compelling structural rationale for this phenomenon. Scholars often attribute these marriages to Justinian’s supposedly romantic, infatuated nature, his desire to bridge the gap with the turbulent circus factions (the Blues and Greens), or simply dismiss it as a bizarre historical quirk documented by a hostile and paranoid Procopius.For standard historiographical attempts to rationalize this marriage, ranging from genuine romantic devotion to calculated political outreach toward the demes (circus factions) and Monophysites, see J. A. S. Evans, The Empress Theodora: Partner of Justinian (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002), pp. 13-27. Evans navigates the tension between Procopius's scandalous assertions and the pragmatic necessities of Justinian's early reign.

div.head: 7.5.2 The Re-emergence of the E-Anna Engine
div.p: Analyzed through the dual sovereignty framework, however, the anomaly vanishes. The marriages to Theodora and Antonina were not romantic eccentricities; they were the precise, structural re-activation of the E-Anna mimetic engine within the Byzantine state. Justinian belonged to an upstart dynasty of lowly peasant origins (via his uncle Justin I)For the humble, provincial origins of the Justinianic dynasty—beginning with Justin I, an Illyrian peasant who rose through the ranks of the imperial guard (the Excubitors)—and the resulting lack of traditional aristocratic capital, see John Moorhead, Justinian (London: Longman, 1994), pp. 1-5.; he lacked the established, multi-generational dynastic capital required to command the unquestioned loyalty of the old aristocratic elites. To execute his staggeringly ambitious military reconquest of the Western Mediterranean, he desperately required the kinetic, charismatic surplus of the BDMB archetype.

Because the Byzantine state operated officially in the black—where overt worship of a martial-erotic goddess like Ishtar or Venus Victrix was theologically impossible—the E-Anna dynamic had to be generated covertly. Theodora and Antonina, emerging from the deeply theatrical, physically transgressive world of the HippodromeOn the late antique theatrical milieu, where actresses and dancers were legally marginalized and inextricably linked with prostitution and moral subversion in the public and ecclesiastical imagination, see Ruth Webb, Demons and Dancers: Performance in Late Antiquity (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2008), pp. 50-80., perfectly embodied the raw, scandalous, boundary-breaking energy of the porneia. By elevating these prostitutes to the pinnacle of power, Justinian and Belisarius forcefully injected the terrifying, charismatic allure of the E-Anna directly into the imperial core.

div.head: 7.5.3 The Thermodynamic Engine of the Reconquest
div.p: This covert synthesis—the impeccable Kullaba legalism of Justinian operating in tandem with the terrifying, mimetic gravitational pull of Theodora—fueled the only period in Byzantine history characterized by aggressive, expansionist, and ultimately unsustainable military reconquest.For the ideological imperative and military dimensions of Justinian's Renovatio Imperii (the recovery of the lost Western provinces), and the staggering material and demographic toll it exacted upon the Byzantine state, see Michael Maas, ed., The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2005), pp. 17-25. Theodora did not merely sit in the palace; as Procopius's Secret History inadvertently reveals (despite its vitriolic hostility), she operated an immense, covert intelligence and patronage network that bypassed the official bureaucracy, terrorizing the elite and demanding absolute, mimetic submission.

Similarly, Antonina accompanied Belisarius on his military campaigns, providing the necessary charismatic aura to bind the loyalty of his diverse, multi-ethnic mercenary armies (bucellarii). The E-Anna engine, running covertly through these powerful women, generated the necessary thermodynamic thrust to conquer North Africa and Italy. However, exactly like the overt Ishtarian empires before it, this engine ran dangerously hot. The attempt to simultaneously maintain the massive Kullaba bureaucracy in the East and fuel the E-Anna warbands in the West proved thermodynamically impossible, exhausting the empire's resources and leaving it critically vulnerable to the subsequent Islamic expansion.
